categories.name: CNS Depressants
categories.desc: Slow the operation of the brain. Includes alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB, Soma, many antidepressants and antipsychotics.

categories.name: CNS Stimulants
categories.desc: Accelerate the heart and brain. Includes cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine, methylphenidate and synthetic cathinones.

categories.name: Hallucinogens
categories.desc: Alter perception, sensation, thinking and emotion. Includes LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, DMT and MDMA.

categories.name: Dissociative Anesthetics
categories.desc: Inhibit pain by cutting off or dissociating the brain’s perception of pain. Includes PCP, its analogs, ketamine and dextromethorphan.

categories.name: Narcotic Analgesics
categories.desc: Relieve pain, induce euphoria and create mood changes. Includes opium derivatives and synthetic opioids such as fentanyl.

categories.name: Inhalants
categories.desc: Breathable chemicals that produce mind-altering results: volatile solvents, aerosols and anesthetic gases.

categories.name: Cannabis
categories.desc: Cannabis sativa products and synthetic cannabinoids. Primary active ingredient delta-9 THC.

footnotes.1: Soma, Quaaludes and some antidepressants usually dilate pupils.
footnotes.2: Quaaludes, alcohol (ETOH) and some antidepressants may elevate pulse.
footnotes.3: Certain psychedelic amphetamines (e.g., MDMA) may cause slowing of reaction to light.
footnotes.4: Pupils normal but may be dilated.
footnotes.5: Blood pressure down with anesthetic gases; up with volatile solvents and aerosols.
footnotes.*: Vertical nystagmus: present with high doses for that individual.

DA: Very early angle of HGN onset
INH: Residue of substance around nose and mouth
CAN: Impaired perception of time and distance

onset.DA: PCP: onset 1–5 min smoked; effects 4–6 h
onset.NA: Heroin: 4–6 h; methadone up to 24 h
onset.INH: Volatile solvents up to 6–8 h; anesthetic gases very short
onset.CAN: Smoked: 2–3 h (impairment may last longer); edibles longer

admin.DA: Smoked, oral, insufflated, injected, eye drops

overdose.DEP: Shallow breathing, clammy skin, dilated pupils, weak rapid pulse, coma
overdose.STI: Agitation, hyperthermia, hallucinations, convulsions, possible death
overdose.HAL: Longer, more intense episodes, psychosis, possible death
overdose.DA: Longer, more intense episodes; hyperthermia; seizures
overdose.NA: Slow shallow breathing, clammy skin, convulsions, coma, possible death
overdose.INH: Coma, sudden sniffing death syndrome (cardiac arrhythmia)

substances.name: Alcohol
substances.dose: ~14 g ethanol per U.S. standard drink
substances.history: The most common impairing substance on U.S. roads; per se limit 0.08 g/dL in 49 states and 0.05 g/dL in Utah (since 2018).

substances.name: Alprazolam
substances.history: FDA approved in 1981. Counterfeit "Xanax bars" pressed with fentanyl or bromazolam are frequently seized.

substances.name: Diazepam
substances.use: Anxiety, muscle spasm, alcohol withdrawal, seizures
substances.history: Introduced by Roche in 1963; among the most prescribed drugs of the 1970s.

substances.name: Clonazepam
substances.history: Long-acting benzodiazepine marketed in the U.S. since 1975.

substances.name: Lorazepam
substances.history: Widely used in hospitals for agitation and seizures.

substances.name: Zolpidem
substances.dose: 5–10 mg at bedtime (5 mg starting dose for women per FDA, 2013)
substances.history: FDA lowered recommended doses in 2013 because of next-morning driving impairment; complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving carry a boxed warning (2019).

substances.name: Carisoprodol
substances.history: Metabolized to meprobamate. Placed in federal Schedule IV in 2012.

substances.name: Methaqualone
substances.history: Popular in the 1970s; moved to Schedule I in 1984.

substances.name: Butalbital (barbiturates)
substances.sched: Schedule III (some combos exempt; phenobarbital IV)
substances.history: Barbiturates were the leading sedatives before benzodiazepines.

substances.name: GHB
substances.dose: Oxybate 4.5–9 g nightly in divided doses
substances.history: Scheduled by the Hillory J. Farias and Samantha Reid Date-Rape Drug Prohibition Act of 2000.

substances.name: Flunitrazepam
substances.use: Not approved in the U.S.; insomnia elsewhere
substances.history: Associated with drug-facilitated sexual assault; the manufacturer reformulated tablets to turn drinks blue.

substances.name: Diphenhydramine
substances.history: First-generation antihistamine; strongly sedating, with anticholinergic effects at high doses that may dilate pupils.

substances.name: Quetiapine
substances.use: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, adjunct for depression
substances.history: Atypical antipsychotic; misused for sedation, including in correctional settings.

substances.name: Trazodone
substances.history: Antidepressant. Some antidepressants may dilate pupils or elevate pulse (Matrix fn 1, 2).

substances.name: Gabapentin
substances.sched: Not federally scheduled (Schedule V in several states)
substances.history: Frequently combined with opioids; several states have scheduled it or require PDMP reporting.

substances.name: Xylazine
substances.sched: Not federally scheduled (scheduled in several states)
substances.history: The White House ONDCP designated fentanyl adulterated with xylazine an emerging threat in April 2023. An alpha-2 agonist, not an opioid; naloxone does not reverse it. Causes severe necrotic wounds.

substances.name: Promethazine
substances.history: Phenothiazine antihistamine; strongly sedating.

substances.name: Baclofen
substances.history: GABA-B agonist; overdose causes coma and respiratory depression.

substances.name: Cyclobenzaprine
substances.history: Structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants; anticholinergic effects may dilate pupils.

substances.name: Bromazolam
substances.history: Novel benzodiazepine found in counterfeit alprazolam and in fentanyl mixtures ("benzo-dope").

substances.name: Phenibut
substances.sched: Not scheduled (FDA: not a lawful dietary supplement)
substances.history: Sold online as a supplement; FDA has issued warning letters.

substances.name: Meprobamate
substances.history: Active metabolite of carisoprodol; the first blockbuster tranquilizer (1955).

substances.name: Cocaine
substances.dose: Illicit: 20–100 mg per line; crack rocks ~0.1 g
substances.history: Isolated from coca leaves in 1860; Schedule II under the Controlled Substances Act of 1970.

substances.name: Methamphetamine
substances.history: Synthesized in Japan in 1919. Current U.S. supply is dominated by high-purity P2P methamphetamine from Mexican cartels (DEA NDTA).

substances.name: Amphetamine (Adderall)
substances.history: Adderall IR approved 1996; national shortages since 2022; counterfeit pills containing meth are reported.

substances.name: Methylphenidate
substances.history: Marketed as Ritalin since 1955.

substances.name: Synthetic cathinones
substances.history: The Synthetic Drug Abuse Prevention Act of 2012 placed several cathinones in Schedule I.

substances.name: Caffeine
substances.dose: Up to ~400 mg/day considered safe for most healthy adults (FDA)
substances.history: The most widely used psychoactive substance in the world. A mild CNS stimulant that is not considered impairing at normal doses.

substances.name: Pseudoephedrine
substances.history: The Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act of 2005 restricts retail sales because it is a methamphetamine precursor.

substances.name: LSD
substances.history: Synthesized by Albert Hofmann in 1938; psychoactive effects discovered in 1943.

substances.name: Psilocybin
substances.sched: Schedule I (federal); regulated access in OR and CO
substances.history: Found in Psilocybe species; Oregon (2020) and Colorado (2022) passed regulated-access measures.

substances.name: Mescaline
substances.sched: Schedule I (religious exemption for Native American Church)
substances.history: From peyote cactus; religious use by members of the Native American Church is protected under 42 U.S.C. § 1996a.

substances.name: DMT
substances.history: Present in many plants; sacramental ayahuasca use was protected in Gonzales v. O Centro (2006).

substances.name: MDMA
substances.use: None (FDA declined approval for PTSD-assisted therapy in 2024)
substances.history: First synthesized by Merck in 1912; placed in Schedule I in 1985.

flags.rtl: May SLOW reaction to light (Matrix fn 3)

substances.name: Salvia divinorum
substances.sched: Not federally scheduled (controlled in many states)
substances.history: A kappa-opioid agonist hallucinogen with very short, intense effects.

substances.name: 2C-B
substances.history: Psychedelic phenethylamine synthesized by Alexander Shulgin in 1974. "Tusi" (pink cocaine) sold under this name usually contains ketamine and MDMA instead.

substances.name: PCP
substances.history: Developed as the anesthetic Sernyl in the 1950s; withdrawn because of post-operative delirium.

substances.name: Ketamine
substances.dose: Anesthetic 1–4.5 mg/kg IV; illicit 30–100 mg snorted
substances.history: Synthesized in 1962 as a shorter-acting PCP analog; FDA approved esketamine nasal spray in 2019.

substances.name: Dextromethorphan
substances.dose: 10–30 mg every 4–8 h (abuse: hundreds of mg)
substances.duration: 6 h or more at high doses
substances.history: At high doses acts as an NMDA antagonist producing dissociative effects similar to PCP; classified by DREs as a dissociative anesthetic.

substances.name: Heroin
substances.history: Synthesized in 1874 and marketed by Bayer in 1898; largely displaced in U.S. markets by fentanyl (DEA NDTA).

substances.name: Fentanyl
substances.history: About 50× more potent than heroin; DEA considers 2 mg a potentially lethal dose and reported in 2023 that 7 of 10 lab-tested counterfeit pills contained a potentially lethal dose.
substances.price: $3–$30 per counterfeit pill (varies by region, DEA NDTA)

substances.name: Oxycodone
substances.history: OxyContin launched in 1996 and was reformulated as abuse-deterrent in 2010.

substances.name: Hydrocodone
substances.history: Combination products were rescheduled from Schedule III to II in October 2014.

substances.name: Morphine
substances.history: Isolated from opium by Friedrich Sertürner around 1804.

substances.name: Codeine
substances.history: "Lean" mixes promethazine-codeine syrup with soda; promethazine adds sedation.

substances.name: Methadone
substances.history: Developed in Germany in the late 1930s; used for opioid maintenance since the 1960s.

substances.name: Buprenorphine
substances.history: Partial mu agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression; the X-waiver was eliminated by the MAT Act (2023).

substances.name: Tramadol
substances.history: Also inhibits serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake; seizure and serotonin-syndrome risk. Federally scheduled in 2014.

substances.name: Hydromorphone
substances.history: Roughly 5× as potent as oral morphine.

substances.name: Nitazenes
substances.dose: Microgram quantities; some analogs exceed fentanyl in potency
substances.history: Benzimidazole opioids developed in the 1950s that re-emerged in illicit markets around 2019.

substances.name: Kratom
substances.sched: Not federally scheduled (banned in some states)
substances.history: DEA proposed temporary scheduling in 2016 and withdrew it; FDA recommended scheduling concentrated 7-OH products in 2025. Low doses act stimulant-like, high doses opioid-like.

substances.name: Cannabis (THC)
substances.sched: Schedule I federally (rescheduling to III proposed 2024)
substances.use: Dronabinol for chemotherapy nausea and AIDS anorexia
substances.duration: 2–3 h smoked; 6–8 h or more for edibles
substances.history: Legal for adult use in about half of U.S. states; no scientifically validated per se THC impairment level exists (NHTSA).

substances.name: Delta-8 THC
substances.sched: Status disputed (hemp-derived under the 2018 Farm Bill)
substances.history: Converted from hemp CBD; products are largely unregulated (FDA consumer warnings 2021–2023).

substances.name: Synthetic cannabinoids
substances.history: Sprayed onto plant material and sold as "incense"; linked to severe agitation, seizures and mass-overdose events.

substances.name: Dronabinol
substances.history: Synthetic THC approved by FDA in 1985.

substances.name: Toluene
substances.sched: Not scheduled (sale restrictions in many states)
substances.duration: Minutes per inhalation; impairment may last hours
substances.history: Chronic use causes permanent cerebellar and peripheral nerve damage.

substances.name: Gasoline
substances.history: A rural and youth abuse pattern; leaded gasoline historically caused lead encephalopathy.

substances.name: Butane / propane
substances.history: A leading cause of sudden sniffing death; can freeze airway tissue when sprayed directly.

substances.name: Nitrous oxide
substances.dose: Balloons from 8 g chargers or tanks
substances.history: Chronic use inactivates vitamin B12 and causes myelopathy; FDA warned in 2025 against flavored products such as "Galaxy Gas".

substances.name: Aerosol propellants
substances.history: Dust removers are common in impaired-driving crashes with the can still in the vehicle; some manufacturers add bittering agents.

substances.name: Alkyl nitrites
substances.rx: Amyl nitrite historically Rx for angina
substances.history: Vasodilators that cause sudden drops in blood pressure and headaches.

substances.name: Acetaminophen
substances.dose: 325–1,000 mg every 4–6 h; max 4 g/day (many labels 3 g)
substances.history: Not impairing. The leading cause of acute liver failure in the U.S. in overdose (antidote: N-acetylcysteine). Often combined with hydrocodone and oxycodone.

substances.name: Ibuprofen
substances.history: NSAID; not impairing.

substances.name: Nicotine
substances.history: Highly addictive; not a DRE category and not evidence of impairment.

caseLaw.s: A warrantless blood draw from a DUI suspect at a hospital was reasonable given exigent circumstances (dissipation of alcohol) and probable cause; blood evidence is physical, not testimonial, so the Fifth Amendment does not bar it.

Natural metabolization of alcohol does not create a per se exigency justifying a nonconsensual warrantless blood test in every DUI case; exigency is decided case by case under the totality of the circumstances.
Warrantless breath tests are permitted as a search incident to a lawful DUI arrest; warrantless blood tests are not. States may not criminally punish refusal of a blood test.
Plurality: when a driver is unconscious and must be taken to a hospital before a breath test can be done, the exigent-circumstances rule almost always permits a warrantless blood test.
Slurred speech and lack of coordination during sobriety tests are non-testimonial physical evidence; routine booking questions fall outside Miranda, but the "sixth birthday" question was testimonial.
Miranda applies to misdemeanor traffic offenses once a suspect is in custody, but roadside questioning during an ordinary traffic stop is not custodial interrogation.
Admitting a suspect’s refusal to submit to a blood-alcohol test into evidence does not violate the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
Random, suspicionless stops of motorists to check licenses and registration violate the Fourth Amendment.

caseLaw.n: Michigan Dept. of State Police v. Sitz
caseLaw.s: Properly conducted sobriety checkpoints are consistent with the Fourth Amendment; the state’s interest in preventing drunk driving outweighs the minimal intrusion.
An officer who learns the registered owner’s license is revoked has reasonable suspicion to stop the vehicle, absent information that the owner is not driving.
A 911 call reporting that a specific vehicle ran the caller off the road gave reasonable suspicion of drunk driving sufficient to justify a stop.

The DRE 12-step protocol and drug-category chart are generally accepted and admissible under Frye when all 12 steps are performed. A qualified DRE may testify that signs are consistent with a drug category but may not claim scientific certainty or predict drug levels.
Testimony by a trained DRE applying the protocol is admissible with foundational safeguards; the officer should avoid language implying scientific certainty.

SFST results are admissible as circumstantial evidence of alcohol consumption and impairment but not as scientific proof of a specific BAC; officers may not use terms like "test," "pass" or "fail" in a scientific sense.

Field sobriety test results had to be administered in strict compliance with standardized procedures to support probable cause; the legislature later adopted a substantial-compliance standard (R.C. 4511.19(D)(4)(b)).
A traffic stop supported by probable cause of a traffic violation is reasonable regardless of the officer’s subjective motivation.
Absent reasonable suspicion, police may not extend a completed traffic stop to conduct a dog sniff.
A dog sniff during a lawful traffic stop that does not prolong it is not a Fourth Amendment search.
Probable cause from a drug-detection dog’s alert is judged by the totality of the circumstances; satisfactory certification or training can establish reliability.
Using a drug-sniffing dog on a home’s front porch is a Fourth Amendment search.
A reasonable mistake of law can support reasonable suspicion for a stop; cocaine found during the ensuing consent search was admissible.
Cocaine found behind a rear-seat armrest gave probable cause to arrest all three occupants of the car.

Police may search a vehicle incident to arrest only if the arrestee is within reaching distance of the passenger compartment or it is reasonable to believe evidence of the offense of arrest is inside.
Established the automobile exception: a vehicle may be searched without a warrant when there is probable cause to believe it contains contraband.
A statute making the status of narcotic addiction a crime violated the Eighth Amendment; the state may punish use or possession, not status.

hgn.en: I am going to check your eyes. Keep your head still and follow the stimulus with your eyes only. Keep following the stimulus with your eyes until I tell you to stop.
hgn.es: Voy a examinar sus ojos. Mantenga la cabeza quieta y siga el estímulo solo con los ojos. Siga el estímulo con los ojos hasta que le diga que se detenga.

wat.en: Place your left foot on the line. Place your right foot on the line ahead of your left foot, with the heel of your right foot against the toe of your left foot. Keep your arms down at your sides. Do not begin until I tell you to. When I tell you to start, take nine heel-to-toe steps up the line, turn, and take nine heel-to-toe steps back down the line. When you turn, keep your front foot on the line and turn by taking a series of small steps with the other foot. Keep your arms at your sides, watch your feet at all times, and count your steps out loud. Once you start walking, do not stop until you have completed the test.
wat.es: Coloque el pie izquierdo sobre la línea. Coloque el pie derecho sobre la línea delante del izquierdo, con el talón del pie derecho contra la punta del pie izquierdo. Mantenga los brazos a los costados. No comience hasta que yo se lo indique. Cuando le diga, dé nueve pasos talón con punta sobre la línea, gire y dé nueve pasos talón con punta de regreso. Al girar, mantenga el pie delantero en la línea y gire con una serie de pasos pequeños con el otro pie. Mantenga los brazos a los costados, mire sus pies en todo momento y cuente sus pasos en voz alta. Una vez que empiece a caminar, no se detenga hasta completar la prueba.

ols.en: Stand with your feet together and your arms down at your sides. Do not begin until I tell you to. When I tell you to, raise one leg, either leg, approximately six inches off the ground, foot pointed out, with both legs straight. Keep your arms at your sides, look at your elevated foot, and count out loud: one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three, and so on, until told to stop.
ols.es: Párese con los pies juntos y los brazos a los costados. No comience hasta que yo se lo indique. Cuando le diga, levante una pierna, cualquiera, aproximadamente seis pulgadas del suelo, con la punta del pie hacia afuera y ambas piernas rectas. Mantenga los brazos a los costados, mire su pie levantado y cuente en voz alta: mil uno, mil dos, mil tres, y así sucesivamente, hasta que le diga que pare.

loc.en: Keep your head still and follow the stimulus with your eyes only. I am going to move it in a circle and then bring it toward the bridge of your nose. Keep your eyes on it.
loc.es: Mantenga la cabeza quieta y siga el estímulo solo con los ojos. Lo voy a mover en un círculo y luego lo acercaré al puente de su nariz. No le quite los ojos de encima.

rom.en: Stand with your feet together and your arms down at your sides. Do not begin until I tell you to. When I tell you to begin, tilt your head back slightly and close your eyes. Keep your head tilted back and your eyes closed until you think thirty seconds have passed, then bring your head forward, open your eyes and say stop.
rom.es: Párese con los pies juntos y los brazos a los costados. No comience hasta que yo se lo indique. Cuando le diga, incline la cabeza ligeramente hacia atrás y cierre los ojos. Manténgase así hasta que crea que han pasado treinta segundos, luego traiga la cabeza hacia adelante, abra los ojos y diga alto.

ftn.en: Stand with your feet together and your arms at your sides. Make a fist with both hands and extend your index fingers, palms forward. When I tell you to begin, tilt your head back slightly and close your eyes. When I call out left or right, touch the tip of that index finger to the tip of your nose, then return your arm to your side.
ftn.es: Párese con los pies juntos y los brazos a los costados. Cierre ambos puños y extienda los dedos índices, con las palmas hacia adelante. Cuando le diga que comience, incline la cabeza ligeramente hacia atrás y cierre los ojos. Cuando yo diga izquierda o derecha, toque la punta de su nariz con la punta de ese dedo índice y luego regrese el brazo a su costado.

steps.d: Instrument, result and time of the evidential breath test.
Driving, contact, SFST results, statements and evidence from the arresting officer.
Medical questions, appearance, eyes, tracking, pupils, HGN check and pulse 1.
HGN per eye with onset angle, vertical gaze nystagmus and lack of convergence.
Modified Romberg, Walk and Turn, One Leg Stand and Finger to Nose.
Blood pressure, body temperature and pulse 2.
Pupil sizes in three lighting conditions, reaction to light, nasal and oral cavity.
Normal, flaccid or rigid, with a body map.
Body map of injection sites and pulse 3.
Miranda, admissions, timeline and other observations.
Matrix-assisted opinion of the drug category or categories.
Specimen, time, laboratory and chain of custody.
